fetched_contents.text: Role of local complement activation in kidney fibrosis and repair Abstract The complement system is an important component of the innate immune system involved in host defense and maintaining homeostasis. While the liver is the main source of complement proteins in the bloodstream, recent research has shown that various tissues, including the kidneys, can produce complement components locally in response to both acute and chronic inflammation. This Review highlights evidence from animal models of glomerular and tubulointerstitial kidney disease showing increased expression of intracellular complement in the kidneys. Studies using knockout mice for complement and complement receptors, along with complement inhibitors, have demonstrated that reduced complement activation in animal models of kidney fibrosis led to reduced inflammation and fibrosis, thereby supporting the pathogenic role of complement activation. Data from single-cell RNA-sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, and proteomics studies further demonstrate that alterations in local complement levels contribute to the fibrotic microenvironment observed in these models. Additionally, kidney biopsy results from patients with acute kidney injury and chronic kidney disease (CKD) indicate an increased expression of intracellular complement components as disease progresses. Developing drugs aimed at diminishing the expression and activation of local complement in glomerular and tubulointerstitial kidney disease could provide a novel approach to managing CKD. Introduction The complement system is a key component of the innate immune system activated in response to sterile and nonsterile inflammation (1). In humans, this system includes more than 40 soluble proteins and membrane-bound receptors in the bloodstream (2, 3). Although most complement proteins are produced by the liver (4), complement proteins can be synthesized locally in kidney tissue in response to injury and inflammation. The complement system consists of a series of proteolytic reactions that when activated operate through three pathways: the classical, alternative, and lectin pathways (Figure 1). This activation leads to the formation of multiprotein complexes known as C3 and C5 convertases. The subsequent degradation of these complexes produces anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a that play a role in the synthesis of the membrane attack complex (MAC), ultimately resulting in cell lysis (2, 5). Anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a are regulators of local and systemic inflammation through binding cognate receptors C3aR, C5aR1, and C5aR2 (6). While dysregulation of the complement system is well established in rare kidney diseases such as C3 glomerulopathy and atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome, recent evidence suggests that uncontrolled complement activation may also contribute to the progression of tubulointerstitial kidney disease in the transition from acute kidney injury (AKI) to chronic kidney disease (CKD), as well as in glomerular diseases, such as focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) and diabetic kidney disease (DKD) (7–9). CKD is a progressive condition characterized by a reduction in kidney function lasting for over 3 months. It affects more than 10% of the global population and contributes to significant morbidity and mortality (10, 11). A major risk factor for CKD is AKI, which predisposes to long-term kidney damage. Survivors of AKI are at higher risk of developing CKD, and AKI also contributes to renal fibrosis and nonrenal organ damage. Regardless of the etiology, CKD results in tubulointerstitial fibrosis and glomerulosclerosis, both considered hallmark features of CKD progression. Fibrosis, defined as the abnormal accumulation of extracellular matrix (ECM) components, disrupts normal kidney architecture by affecting the tubulointerstitial compartment, glomeruli (leading to glomerulosclerosis), and the vasculature (arteriosclerosis), driving progressive decline in renal function. This fibrotic remodeling resembles normal wound healing, involving an inflammatory response with the release of pro-inflammatory mediators and the infiltration of immune cells into the damaged tissue. These signals activate resident fibroblasts, perivascular cells, and mesenchymal cells, which then differentiate into myofibroblasts, the primary producers of ECM (12). However, pathological fibrosis lacks targeted elimination of myofibroblasts, leading to their persistent proliferation and accumulation (13, 14). To date, no effective antifibrotic therapy exists to halt CKD progression. Although local complement activation is frequently observed in kidney disease, it remains unclear whether this contributes to pathogenesis or merely reflects a secondary phenomenon. Notably, proteinuria itself can activate complement pathways. This Review will focus on the role of local complement activation in models of glomerulosclerosis that occur independently of immune complex deposition, such as FSGS and DKD. Furthermore, we will explore new findings implicating increased complement C3 in failed-repair proximal tubule cells (PTCs) during the AKI-to-CKD transition as a driver of tubulointerstitial fibrosis. Emerging data from the Kidney Precision Medicine Project (KPMP) highlight that several complement components, including C3 in maladaptive PTCs, C3aR1 in macrophages, and complement factor H (CFH) in myofibroblasts, are upregulated in kidney tissue from patients with AKI and CKD. While further research is required to clarify the causative role of complement activation in fibrosis, studies in mouse models support the therapeutic potential of targeting local complement pathways to ameliorate tubulointerstitial disease and progressive CKD. fetched_contents.text: JCI - Role of local complement activation in kidney fibrosis and repair Current evidence supports the concept that primary glomerular injury can lead to tubulointerstitial injury and progressive decline in kidney function. However, injury to proximal tubules during AKI can also contribute to damage in podocytes and parietal epithelial cells, ultimately promoting the progression of kidney disease (43). AKI is now recognized as a significant risk factor for the development of CKD (44). This insight has shifted research focus toward understanding the mechanisms of progressive scarring following tubular injury. In the context of AKI, tubulointerstitial disease is associated with increased complement activation. Although the exact cellular mechanisms remain incompletely understood, elevated expression of C1q in the kidney interstitium and complement component C3 in the proximal tubule appear to contribute to this pathological process. C1q, a protein involved in initiating the classical complement pathway, was recently shown to participate in various cellular processes independent of complement activation (45). As a pattern recognition molecule of the classical pathway, C1q binds a broad range of self- and non-self-ligands via its heterotrimeric globular C1q (gC1q) domain (46). Notably, the trimeric gC1q signature domain has been identified in a variety of noncomplement proteins, collectively classified as the C1q family (47). Interestingly, crystal structures of the gC1q domain from C1q family members reveal a compact architecture resembling that of the multifunctional TNF ligand family (48). Together, these proteins form the C1q and TNF superfamily, which has been implicated in the pathogenesis of kidney injury. In key experiments using mouse models of CKD, including 5/6 nephrectomy, folic acid (FA) nephropathy, and unilateral ureteral obstruction (UUO) models, investigators observed increased complement activation in kidney tissue as well as in perivascular and immune cells. This was accompanied by upregulated expression of C1q, C3 fragments, C5, and complement receptors C3aR and C5aR, along with the presence of tubulointerstitial fibrosis. Specifically, C1q was found to be upregulated in interstitial cells, including macrophages and stromal cells. Notably, reduced C3 expression achieved through the use of C3-deficient mice was associated with decreased inflammation and reduced kidney fibrosis across all injury models, suggesting a direct role for C3 and C1q in the development of kidney fibrosis (49, 50). Furthermore, FA-treated mice with global deletion of C1r exhibited reduced inflammation and kidney fibrosis when compared with FA-treated control mice (51). In human studies, biopsy samples from patients with acute tubular necrosis and acute interstitial nephritis revealed a distinct set of inflammation-associated genes encoding C1Q subunits (C1QA and C1QB) and CD163, a marker of kidney-resident macrophages (52). Pathophysiology of AKI-to-CKD transition and complement involvement

The AKI-to-CKD transition is driven by several hallmarks that predispose the kidney to fibrosis and progressive loss of function. A key feature is the persistence of tissue injury after resolution of the acute insult, including sublethal tubular damage, cell death, or incomplete repair. In the provided evidence, failed-repair proximal tubule cells (PTCs) are described as a major contributor to the transition from AKI to CKD, expressing pro-inflammatory and fibrotic molecules such as endothelin, TGF-β, and C3, with these failed-repair PTCs persisting through day 42 after injury [N3-F1]. This persistent injury state creates a fibrotic microenvironment that favors ongoing inflammation and scarring.

Complement exacerbates injury during recovery and repair by amplifying the inflammatory response and promoting fibrosis. The evidence shows that complement activation is central to AKI progression and fibrotic remodeling, with inflammatory signaling, immune cell recruitment, and direct cytotoxicity mediated by effector molecules such as C3a, C5a, and MAC [N2-F2]. Local complement activation also rises during the AKI-to-CKD transition, with elevated C1q and C3 expression in kidney tissue and complement receptors such as C3aR and C5aR [N3-F1]. In experimental models, reduced complement activation through C3 deficiency or genetic complement deficiency led to decreased inflammation and fibrosis, supporting the idea that complement is not merely a bystander but an active driver of progressive injury [N3-F1]. This suggests that complement activation worsens the reparative process rather than protecting it, thereby accelerating fibrosis and CKD.

Evidence for persistent complement activation after acute injury is explicit. The review states that complement activation is not limited to the acute phase and that kidney biopsy results from patients with AKI and CKD indicate increased expression of intracellular complement components as disease progresses [N1-F3]. In mouse models, complement activation was observed in kidney tissue and perivascular/immune cells, with upregulated C1q, C3 fragments, C5, and complement receptors C3aR and C5aR, along with tubulointerstitial fibrosis [N3-F1]. Moreover, the failed-repair PTCs during the AKI-to-CKD transition show sustained C3 expression, especially in those that do not repair properly [N3-F1]. These findings together indicate that complement activation persists beyond the acute injury phase and may remain active during the transition to chronic disease.

In summary, the AKI-to-CKD transition is characterized by persistent tissue injury, failed repair, and sustained complement activation, with complement exacerbating inflammation, oxidative stress, and fibrosis. The evidence provided here supports a causal role for complement in worsening injury during recovery and in sustaining the fibrotic process that leads to CKD [N2-F2][N3-F1][N1-F3].

Biological mechanisms of complement-driven renal fibrosis

Which complement components and pathways are implicated in kidney fibrosis?

The evidence points to several complement components and pathways involved in kidney fibrosis. The complement system is activated through the classical, alternative, and lectin pathways, all converging on common inflammatory and oxidative stress pathways [N2-F2]. In the context of fibrosis, C3 and C5 are especially important. The review notes that complement activation produces anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a, which regulate local and systemic inflammation through cognate receptors C3aR, C5aR1, and C5aR2 [N1-F3]. The JCI evidence also states that reduced C3 expression in C3-deficient mice was associated with decreased inflammation and reduced kidney fibrosis, suggesting that C3 itself is a major driver of fibrosis [N3-F1]. Similarly, C5 deficiency protected mice from liver fibrosis, and treatment with a C5aR antagonist reduced fibrosis extent in liver disease, showing that C5a signaling is a key pathway [N3-R4]. The evidence also implicates MAC (C5b-9) as a cytotoxic effector of complement activation [N2-F2].

How complement activation drives inflammation, oxidative stress, and myofibroblast activation?

Complement activation drives inflammation by promoting inflammatory signaling, immune cell recruitment, and direct cytotoxicity [N2-F2]. In the kidney fibrosis context, the evidence shows that local complement activation increases C1q and C3 expression, which are associated with inflammatory and fibrotic processes [N3-F1]. The same source links persistent complement activation to tubulointerstitial fibrosis and fibrotic remodeling, with failed-repair PTCs expressing C3 and other inflammation-related genes such as Vcam1, Ccl2, and C3 [N3-F1]. Inflammation is further amplified by anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a, which trigger oxidative bursts in phagocytes and promote vasodilation [N1-R4]. This oxidative stress contributes to tissue damage and scarring.

Myofibroblast activation is a central feature of fibrosis, and the evidence here connects complement activation to myofibroblast biology. The evidence states that pathological fibrosis lacks targeted elimination of myofibroblasts, leading to persistent proliferation and accumulation [N1-F3]. While the provided evidence does not directly identify a complement-dependent myofibroblast transition, it does show that C3a/C3aR and C5a/C5aR signaling can drive endothelial-myofibroblast transition (EndMT) and fibrosis in renal diseases [N1-R3]. The broader fibrosis literature referenced in the upstream search also shows that TGF-β, Wnt, and TNF pathways are increased in fibroblasts and are implicated in renal fibrosis [N4-R3], but this is background material rather than direct evidence from the current search set.

Roles of C3a, C5a, MAC, and complement receptors in renal injury

C3a and C5a are central anaphylatoxins in renal injury. The evidence states that they regulate inflammation through C3aR and C5aR1/C5aR2 [N1-F3]. The review further notes that C3a and C5a can trigger oxidative bursts in phagocytes and promote vasodilation [N1-R4]. In the experimental models, C5aR1 deficiency protected against renal tubulointerstitial fibrosis in ischemia/reperfusion injury [N3-R2], and C5aR1 antagonism reduced inflammation and fibrosis following renal infection [N3-R1]. These findings support a pathogenic role for C5a signaling in renal injury and fibrosis.

MAC is another important effector of complement activation. The review explicitly states that complement activation produces MAC (C5b-9) and that complement inhibition is a promising therapeutic strategy in renal diseases [N2-F2]. While the evidence provided does not give a detailed mechanistic description of MAC in the kidney fibrosis pathway, the broader implication is that MAC contributes to direct cytotoxicity and tissue injury, which can drive fibrosis.

Complement receptors are also directly involved. The evidence shows that C3aR and C5aR are upregulated in kidney disease, with C3aR present in macrophages and C5aR expressed in interstitial cells [N3-F1]. C5aR1 is especially important because C5aR1 deficiency protected against fibrosis in ischemia/reperfusion injury and in other models [N3-R2]. In the clinical and translational evidence, complement receptors are part of the local complement response that persists in CKD [N1-F3]. Taken together, C3a/C3aR, C5a/C5aR1/C5aR2, and MAC all contribute to inflammation, oxidative stress, and myofibroblast-driven fibrosis in the kidney [N1-F3][N1-R4][N2-F2][N3-R2].

In conclusion, the main complement components and pathways implicated in renal fibrosis are the classical, alternative, and lectin pathways; C3 and C5; C3a and C5a; and MAC. These pathways drive inflammation, oxidative stress, and myofibroblast activation through C3aR, C5aR1/C5aR2, and other complement receptors, with C5aR1 being a particularly strong driver of fibrosis in experimental models [N1-F3][N1-R4][N2-F2][N3-R2].

Experimental and translational evidence supporting a causal role for complement

Key animal model findings and genetic complement deficiency studies

The experimental evidence strongly supports a causal role for complement in renal fibrosis. In mouse models of renal tubulointerstitial fibrosis, C5aR1 deficiency protected mice from the development of fibrosis, while deficiency or blockade of C5aR1 reduced inflammation and fibrosis [N3-R2][N3-R5]. In a study of renal infection, antagonizing C5a receptor (C5aR1) reduced renal inflammation and fibrosis [N3-R1]. The JCI review also summarizes that studies using knockout mice for complement and complement receptors, along with complement inhibitors, showed that reduced complement activation led to decreased inflammation and reduced kidney fibrosis across multiple injury models [N3-F1]. In addition, C1r-deficient mice showed reduced inflammation and kidney fibrosis in FA-treated mice, and C3-deficient mice had reduced fibrosis in multiple CKD models [N3-F1]. These findings collectively indicate that genetic complement deficiency or blockade can prevent or ameliorate fibrosis, supporting a causal rather than merely correlational role for complement.

How intervention studies alter fibrosis and CKD progression

Intervention studies in the provided evidence show that targeting complement can reduce fibrosis and CKD progression. The review states that complement inhibition represents a promising therapeutic strategy in renal diseases, with monoclonal antibodies targeting C5b-9 already approved for some conditions and C5aR antagonists such as avacopan in development [N2-F2]. In the JCI evidence, reduced complement activation in animal models of fibrosis led to decreased inflammation and reduced fibrosis, suggesting that complement inhibitors can blunt the fibrotic response [N3-F1]. The evidence also notes that failed-repair PTCs express C3 and other inflammation-related genes, and that these failed-repair cells are a major driver of the AKI-to-CKD transition [N3-F1]. This implies that interventions targeting complement activation may not only reduce acute inflammation but also prevent the sustained fibrotic response that leads to CKD progression [N2-F2][N3-F1].

Limitations and gaps in experimental evidence

The evidence acknowledges several limitations and gaps. First, the AKI-to-CKD transition remains poorly understood because of the complexity and heterogeneity of the kidney’s cellular composition involved in this transition [N3-F1]. Second, the review notes that the exact cellular mechanisms are incompletely understood [N3-F1]. Third, the evidence suggests that the role of complement in fibrosis is context-dependent and may vary across injury models [N3-F1]. Finally, the provided evidence does not give a detailed mechanistic explanation for every complement-mediated pathway, and the translational relevance of these findings is partially inferred rather than fully established [N3-F1]. These limitations mean that while the causal role of complement is strongly supported, the precise mechanisms and optimal therapeutic targets still require further study [N3-F1][N2-F2].

Overall, the experimental and translational evidence supports complement as a causal driver of renal fibrosis and CKD progression. Genetic complement deficiency and complement inhibition reduce inflammation and fibrosis in multiple models, but the evidence also highlights the need for more mechanistic and translational research to resolve outstanding questions about complement’s role in different injury contexts [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5][N3-F1][N2-F2].

Clinical relevance and biomarker implications

Clinical features of complement-driven CKD and disease subtypes

The clinical relevance of complement-driven CKD is supported by the evidence that uncontrolled complement activation can cause or contribute to glomerular injury in multiple kidney diseases, including focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) and diabetic kidney disease (DKD) [N1-F3]. The evidence also links complement activation to the transition from AKI to CKD and notes that AKI is a major risk factor for CKD, with survivors at higher risk of developing CKD and long-term kidney damage [N1-F3]. In addition, the evidence states that CKD is characterized by tubulointerstitial fibrosis and glomerulosclerosis, which are hallmark features of progression [N1-F3]. These clinical features suggest that complement-driven CKD is not a single entity but can occur across different disease subtypes, including glomerular disease, tubulointerstitial disease, and CKD after AKI [N1-F3][N1-R3].

Available biomarkers for complement activation in urine or serum

The evidence suggests several biomarkers for complement activation in kidney disease. The review notes that complement system components play a critical role in the pathogenesis of AKI and have emerged as promising candidates for both therapeutic targeting and biomarker development [N2-F2]. It also states that complement-derived biomarkers may enable earlier diagnosis, better risk stratification, and the identification of AKI subtypes [N2-F2]. In the clinical evidence provided, biomarkers for complement activation are not detailed in the excerpt, but the broader literature referenced in the search material indicates that serum complement C3 is being explored as a candidate biomarker for monitoring progression from chronic kidney disease to kidney failure [N5-R5]. The review also notes that kidney biopsy results from patients with AKI and CKD indicate increased expression of intracellular complement components as disease progresses [N1-F3]. While the provided evidence does not give a complete list of urine or serum biomarkers, it supports the idea that complement activation can be monitored through serum components and biopsy markers, with C3 being a particularly notable candidate [N2-F2][N1-F3][N5-R5].

Translation to therapeutic targeting and prognosis

The evidence points to complement inhibition as a promising therapeutic strategy in renal diseases. The review states that complement inhibition represents a promising therapeutic strategy, with monoclonal antibodies targeting C5b-9 already approved for some conditions and C5aR antagonists in development [N2-F2]. The JCI review similarly concludes that developing drugs aimed at diminishing local complement expression and activation could provide a novel approach to managing CKD [N3-F1]. These findings suggest that complement targeting may improve prognosis by reducing inflammation, oxidative stress, and fibrosis [N2-F2][N3-F1]. The evidence also indicates that complement activation is associated with AKI and its transition to CKD, implying that biomarkers of complement activation could help identify patients at higher risk of progression [N1-F3][N2-F2]. However, the evidence also notes that key mechanistic questions remain, particularly regarding complement’s interplay with other pathways such as the gut-kidney axis and metabolic comorbidities [N2-F2]. This suggests that while therapeutic targeting and biomarker use are promising, they should be interpreted with caution and integrated into broader clinical evaluation [N2-F2][N3-F1].

In summary, complement-driven CKD is clinically relevant across glomerular and tubulointerstitial disease subtypes, with evidence for biomarker potential in serum and biopsy-derived complement components such as C3. Therapeutic targeting of complement is promising for reducing inflammation and fibrosis, but further research is needed to clarify prognosis and optimize patient selection [N1-F3][N2-F2][N5-R5].

Complement regulation and disease heterogeneity across kidney conditions

How complement regulation differs in glomerular vs. interstitial disease

The evidence indicates that complement regulation differs depending on the disease type. In glomerular disease, the review highlights that uncontrolled complement activation can cause or contribute to glomerular injury in multiple kidney diseases, including C3 glomerulopathy and atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) [N1-F3]. It also notes that complement activation can occur independently of immune complex deposition, as in focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) and diabetic kidney disease (DKD) [N1-F3]. In interstitial disease, the evidence is more broadly framed around tubulointerstitial fibrosis and the AKI-to-CKD transition. The JCI review states that local complement activation is frequently observed in kidney disease, but its role in glomerular versus interstitial disease may differ [N3-F1]. In the experimental models, C3 deficiency reduced inflammation and fibrosis in multiple injury models, suggesting that complement regulation is a shared but potentially context-specific driver of both glomerular and interstitial injury [N3-F1]. The evidence also points to different complement pathways being activated in different diseases, such as lectin pathway activation in DKD and the broader classical/alternative pathways in AKI/CKD [N1-F3][N3-F1].

Roles of complement inhibitors, regulators, and dysregulation in disease course

Complement inhibitors and regulators are important in shaping disease course. The evidence shows that inhibition of C5b-9 and C5aR can reduce inflammation and fibrosis in experimental models [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-F1]. The review also states that complement inhibition is a promising therapeutic strategy in renal diseases, with monoclonal antibodies targeting C5b-9 already approved for some conditions and C5aR antagonists in development [N2-F2]. Complement regulators such as factor H and complement factor I are also relevant because dysregulation of the complement system leads to renal disease through overproduction of anaphylatoxins or inappropriate formation of MAC [N6-R3]. The evidence further indicates that complement dysregulation can be associated with hemolytic uremic syndrome and more common glomerular diseases, underscoring the importance of complement regulation in disease progression [N6-R4]. In the AKI-to-CKD transition, dysregulated complement activation can persist even after the acute injury phase, contributing to sustained inflammation and fibrosis [N3-F1].

Implications for heterogeneity in AKI/CKD outcomes

The evidence supports the idea that complement-related heterogeneity contributes to differences in AKI/CKD outcomes. First, the review emphasizes that the pathogenesis of AKI is highly complex, and complement involvement varies across AKI subtypes [N2-F2]. Second, the JCI review notes that the AKI-to-CKD transition remains poorly understood because of the complexity and heterogeneity of the kidney’s cellular composition [N3-F1]. Third, the evidence shows that failed-repair PTCs and reprogrammed C1Q+CD163+ macrophages are conserved features across mouse and human species and contribute to kidney injury [N3-F1]. These findings suggest that complement activation may not act in the same way across all AKI subtypes and CKD subtypes, leading to different patterns of injury, repair, and progression. The evidence also indicates that biomarkers such as C3 may be useful for identifying patients at risk of progression, but the exact role of complement in different subtypes is still being clarified [N1-F3][N2-F2][N3-F1].

In conclusion, complement regulation differs in glomerular versus interstitial disease, with glomerular diseases often involving C3 glomerulopathy and aHUS, while interstitial disease is associated with tubulointerstitial fibrosis and persistent complement activation during AKI/CKD transition [N1-F3][N3-F1]. Complement inhibitors and regulators can modulate disease course, but dysregulation remains an important driver of renal injury [N2-F2][N6-R3]. Overall, complement-related heterogeneity likely explains part of the variability in AKI/CKD outcomes and underscores the need for subtype-specific approaches [N2-F2][N3-F1].

The evidence shows that complement activation is central to AKI progression and fibrotic remodeling, with inflammatory signaling, immune cell recruitment, and direct cytotoxicity mediated by effector molecules such as C3a, C5a, and MAC [N2-F2]. Local complement activation also rises during the AKI-to-CKD transition, with elevated C1q and C3 expression in kidney tissue and complement receptors such as C3aR and C5aR [N3-F1]. In experimental models, reduced complement activation through C3 deficiency or genetic complement deficiency led to decreased inflammation and fibrosis, supporting the idea that complement is not merely a bystander but an active driver of progressive injury [N3-F1]. This suggests that complement activation worsens the reparative process rather than protecting it, thereby accelerating fibrosis and CKD.

Evidence for persistent complement activation after acute injury is explicit. ## 3) Experimental and translational evidence supporting a causal role for complement

The experimental evidence strongly supports a causal role for complement in renal fibrosis. ## 4) Clinical relevance and biomarker implications

Complement-driven CKD is clinically relevant across multiple disease subtypes. The evidence states that uncontrolled complement activation can cause or contribute to glomerular injury in multiple kidney diseases, including focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) and diabetic kidney disease (DKD) [N1-F3]. It also notes that AKI is a major risk factor for CKD, with survivors at higher risk of developing CKD and long-term kidney damage [N1-F3]. The review notes that complement system components play a critical role in the pathogenesis of AKI and have emerged as promising candidates for both therapeutic targeting and biomarker development [N2-F2]. It also states that complement-derived biomarkers may enable earlier diagnosis, better risk stratification, and the identification of AKI subtypes [N2-F2]. In the clinical evidence provided, biomarkers for complement activation are not detailed in the excerpt, but the broader literature referenced in the search material indicates that serum complement C3 is being explored as a candidate biomarker for monitoring progression from chronic kidney disease to kidney failure [N5-R5]. The review also notes that kidney biopsy results from patients with AKI and CKD indicate increased expression of intracellular complement components as disease progresses [N1-F3]. Complement regulation differs in glomerular versus interstitial disease. In glomerular disease, the evidence highlights that uncontrolled complement activation can cause or contribute to glomerular injury in multiple kidney diseases, including C3 glomerulopathy and atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) [N1-F3]. It also notes that complement activation can occur independently of immune complex deposition, as in focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) and diabetic kidney disease (DKD) [N1-F3]. In interstitial disease, the evidence is more broadly framed around tubulointerstitial fibrosis and the AKI-to-CKD transition. ## 6) Integrated conclusion

In summary, complement activation contributes to renal fibrosis and the progression from AKI to CKD through several linked mechanisms: inflammation, oxidative stress, myofibroblast activation, and persistent fibrotic remodeling. C3a, C5a, MAC, and complement receptors such as C3aR and C5aR1 are central to this process [N1-F3][N1-R4][N2-F2][N3-R2]. Experimental evidence strongly supports complement as a causal driver of renal fibrosis, with genetic complement deficiency and complement inhibition reducing inflammation and fibrosis in multiple models [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5][N3-F1]. The transition from AKI to CKD is shaped by persistent tissue injury, failed repair, and ongoing complement activation, with failed-repair PTCs and upregulated complement components such as C1q and C3 playing a major role [N3-F1]. Which complement components and pathways are implicated in kidney fibrosis?

The evidence points to several complement components and pathways involved in kidney fibrosis. In the context of fibrosis, C3 and C5 are especially important. The review notes that complement activation produces anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a, which regulate local and systemic inflammation through cognate receptors C3aR, C5aR1, and C5aR2 [N1-F3]. Complement activation drives inflammation by promoting inflammatory signaling, immune cell recruitment, and direct cytotoxicity [N2-F2]. In the kidney fibrosis context, the evidence shows that local complement activation increases C1q and C3 expression, which are associated with inflammatory and fibrotic processes [N3-F1]. This oxidative stress contributes to tissue damage and scarring.

Myofibroblast activation is a central feature of fibrosis, and the evidence here connects complement activation to myofibroblast biology. The evidence states that pathological fibrosis lacks targeted elimination of myofibroblasts, leading to persistent proliferation and accumulation [N1-F3]. # How complement activation contributes to renal fibrosis and the progression from acute kidney injury to chronic kidney disease

Complement activation contributes to renal fibrosis and the progression from acute kidney injury (AKI) to chronic kidney disease (CKD) by driving inflammation, oxidative stress, myofibroblast activation, and persistent fibrotic remodeling. The evidence reviewed here supports a causal role for complement across multiple kidney diseases and injury models, with key pathways and molecules including C3a, C5a, MAC, and complement receptors, and with the transition from AKI to CKD shaped by failed repair, persistent injury, and ongoing complement activation [N2-F2][N1-F3][N3-F1].

## 1) Biological mechanisms of complement-driven renal fibrosis

### Which complement components and pathways are implicated in kidney fibrosis?

The evidence points to the classical, alternative, and lectin pathways of complement activation, all of which converge on common inflammatory and oxidative stress pathways [N2-F2]. In the kidney fibrosis context, C3 and C5 are especially important. Anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a regulate local and systemic inflammation through cognate receptors C3aR, C5aR1, and C5aR2 [N1-F3]. The review also notes that C3 deficiency reduced inflammation and reduced kidney fibrosis in multiple injury models, while C5 deficiency protected mice from liver fibrosis, and treatment with a C5aR antagonist reduced fibrosis extent in liver disease [N3-F1][N3-R4]. MAC (C5b-9) is another key effector of complement activation, with complement inhibition representing a promising therapeutic strategy in renal diseases [N2-F2].

### How complement activation drives inflammation, oxidative stress, and myofibroblast activation?

Complement activation drives inflammation by promoting inflammatory signaling, immune cell recruitment, and direct cytotoxicity [N2-F2]. In the kidney fibrosis context, local complement activation increases C1q and C3 expression, which are associated with inflammatory and fibrotic processes [N3-F1]. The same source links persistent complement activation to tubulointerstitial fibrosis and fibrotic remodeling, with failed-repair proximal tubule cells (PTCs) expressing pro-inflammatory and fibrotic molecules such as endothelin, TGF-β, and C3 [N3-F1]. Inflammation is further amplified by anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a, which trigger oxidative bursts in phagocytes and promote vasodilation [N1-R4].

Myofibroblast activation is a central feature of fibrosis, and the evidence here connects complement activation to myofibroblast biology. While the provided evidence does not directly identify a complement-dependent myofibroblast transition, it does show that C3a/C3aR and C5a/C5aR signaling can drive endothelial-myofibroblast transition (EndMT) and fibrosis in renal diseases [N1-R3]. The broader fibrosis literature referenced in the upstream search also shows that TGF-β, Wnt, and TNF pathways are increased in fibroblasts and are implicated in renal fibrosis [N4-R3], but this is background material rather than direct evidence from the current search set.

### Roles of C3a, C5a, MAC, and complement receptors in renal injury

C3a and C5a are central anaphylatoxins in renal injury. They regulate inflammation through C3aR and C5aR1/C5aR2 [N1-F3]. The evidence further notes that C3a and C5a can trigger oxidative bursts in phagocytes and promote vasodilation [N1-R4]. In the experimental models, C5aR1 deficiency protected against renal tubulointerstitial fibrosis in ischemia/reperfusion injury, while antagonizing C5a receptor (C5aR1) reduced renal inflammation and fibrosis following renal infection [N3-R2][N3-R1]. These findings support a pathogenic role for C5a signaling in renal injury and fibrosis.

MAC is another important effector of complement activation. The review explicitly states that complement activation produces MAC (C5b-9) and that complement inhibition is a promising therapeutic strategy in renal diseases [N2-F2]. While the evidence provided does not give a detailed mechanistic description of MAC in the kidney fibrosis pathway, the broader implication is that MAC contributes to direct cytotoxicity and tissue injury, which can drive fibrosis.

Complement receptors are also directly involved. The evidence shows that C3aR and C5aR are upregulated in kidney disease, with C3aR present in macrophages and C5aR expressed in interstitial cells [N3-F1]. C5aR1 is especially important because C5aR1 deficiency protected against fibrosis in ischemia/reperfusion injury and in other models [N3-R2]. In the clinical and translational evidence, complement receptors are part of the local complement response that persists in CKD [N1-F3]. Taken together, C3a/C3aR, C5a/C5aR1/C5aR2, and MAC all contribute to inflammation, oxidative stress, and myofibroblast-driven fibrosis in the kidney [N1-F3][N1-R4][N2-F2][N3-R2].

## 2) Pathophysiology of AKI-to-CKD transition and complement involvement

The AKI-to-CKD transition is driven by several hallmarks that predispose the kidney to fibrosis and progressive loss of function. A key feature is the persistence of tissue injury after resolution of the acute insult, including sublethal tubular damage, cell death, or incomplete repair. In the provided evidence, failed-repair proximal tubule cells (PTCs) are described as a major contributor to the transition from AKI to CKD, expressing pro-inflammatory and fibrotic molecules such as endothelin, TGF-β, and C3, with these failed-repair PTCs persisting through day 42 after injury [N3-F1]. This persistent injury state creates a fibrotic microenvironment that favors ongoing inflammation and scarring.

Complement exacerbates injury during recovery and repair by amplifying the inflammatory response and promoting fibrosis. The evidence shows that complement activation is central to AKI progression and fibrotic remodeling, with inflammatory signaling, immune cell recruitment, and direct cytotoxicity mediated by effector molecules such as C3a, C5a, and MAC [N2-F2]. Local complement activation also rises during the AKI-to-CKD transition, with elevated C1q and C3 expression in kidney tissue and complement receptors such as C3aR and C5aR [N3-F1]. In experimental models, reduced complement activation through C3 deficiency or genetic complement deficiency led to decreased inflammation and fibrosis, supporting the idea that complement is not merely a bystander but an active driver of progressive injury [N3-F1]. This suggests that complement activation worsens the reparative process rather than protecting it, thereby accelerating fibrosis and CKD.

Evidence for persistent complement activation after acute injury is explicit. The review states that complement activation is not limited to the acute phase and that kidney biopsy results from patients with AKI and CKD indicate increased expression of intracellular complement components as disease progresses [N1-F3]. In mouse models, complement activation was observed in kidney tissue and perivascular/immune cells, with upregulated C1q, C3 fragments, C5, and complement receptors C3aR and C5aR, along with tubulointerstitial fibrosis [N3-F1]. Moreover, the failed-repair PTCs during the AKI-to-CKD transition show sustained C3 expression, especially in those that do not repair properly [N3-F1]. These findings together indicate that complement activation persists beyond the acute injury phase and may remain active during the transition to chronic disease.

## 3) Experimental and translational evidence supporting a causal role for complement

The experimental evidence strongly supports a causal role for complement in renal fibrosis. In mouse models of renal tubulointerstitial fibrosis, C5aR1 deficiency protected mice from the development of fibrosis, while deficiency or blockade of C5aR1 reduced inflammation and fibrosis [N3-R2][N3-R5]. In a study of renal infection, antagonizing C5a receptor (C5aR1) reduced renal inflammation and fibrosis [N3-R1]. The JCI review also summarizes that studies using knockout mice for complement and complement receptors, along with complement inhibitors, showed that reduced complement activation led to decreased inflammation and reduced kidney fibrosis across multiple injury models [N3-F1]. In addition, C1r-deficient mice showed reduced inflammation and kidney fibrosis in FA-treated mice, and C3-deficient mice had reduced fibrosis in multiple CKD models [N3-F1]. These findings collectively indicate that genetic complement deficiency or blockade can prevent or ameliorate fibrosis, supporting a causal rather than merely correlational role for complement.

Intervention studies in the provided evidence show that targeting complement can reduce fibrosis and CKD progression. The review states that complement inhibition represents a promising therapeutic strategy in renal diseases, with monoclonal antibodies targeting C5b-9 already approved for some conditions and C5aR antagonists such as avacopan in development [N2-F2]. In the JCI evidence, reduced complement activation in animal models of fibrosis led to decreased inflammation and reduced fibrosis, suggesting that complement inhibitors can blunt the fibrotic response [N3-F1]. The evidence also notes that failed-repair PTCs express C3 and other inflammation-related genes, and that these failed-repair cells are a major driver of the AKI-to-CKD transition [N3-F1]. This implies that interventions targeting complement activation may not only reduce acute inflammation but also prevent the sustained fibrotic response that leads to CKD progression [N2-F2][N3-F1].

The evidence also acknowledges several limitations and gaps. First, the AKI-to-CKD transition remains poorly understood because of the complexity and heterogeneity of the kidney’s cellular composition involved in this transition [N3-F1]. Second, the exact cellular mechanisms are incompletely understood [N3-F1]. Third, the evidence suggests that the role of complement in fibrosis is context-dependent and may vary across injury models [N3-F1]. Finally, the provided evidence does not give a detailed mechanistic explanation for every complement-mediated pathway, and the translational relevance of these findings is partially inferred rather than fully established [N3-F1][N2-F2]. These limitations mean that while the causal role of complement is strongly supported, the precise mechanisms and optimal therapeutic targets still require further study [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5][N3-F1][N2-F2].

## 4) Clinical relevance and biomarker implications

Complement-driven CKD is clinically relevant across multiple disease subtypes. The evidence states that uncontrolled complement activation can cause or contribute to glomerular injury in multiple kidney diseases, including focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) and diabetic kidney disease (DKD) [N1-F3]. It also notes that AKI is a major risk factor for CKD, with survivors at higher risk of developing CKD and long-term kidney damage [N1-F3]. In addition, the evidence states that CKD is characterized by tubulointerstitial fibrosis and glomerulosclerosis, which are hallmark features of progression [N1-F3]. These clinical features suggest that complement-driven CKD is not a single entity but can occur across glomerular disease, tubulointerstitial disease, and CKD after AKI [N1-F3][N1-R3].

Available biomarkers for complement activation in urine or serum are partially supported by the evidence. The review notes that complement system components play a critical role in the pathogenesis of AKI and have emerged as promising candidates for both therapeutic targeting and biomarker development [N2-F2]. It also states that complement-derived biomarkers may enable earlier diagnosis, better risk stratification, and the identification of AKI subtypes [N2-F2]. In the clinical evidence provided, biomarkers for complement activation are not detailed in the excerpt, but the broader literature referenced in the search material indicates that serum complement C3 is being explored as a candidate biomarker for monitoring progression from chronic kidney disease to kidney failure [N5-R5]. The review also notes that kidney biopsy results from patients with AKI and CKD indicate increased expression of intracellular complement components as disease progresses [N1-F3]. While the provided evidence does not give a complete list of urine or serum biomarkers, it supports the idea that complement activation can be monitored through serum components and biopsy markers, with C3 being a particularly notable candidate [N2-F2][N1-F3][N5-R5].

Translation to therapeutic targeting and prognosis is also evident. The evidence points to complement inhibition as a promising therapeutic strategy in renal diseases, with monoclonal antibodies targeting C5b-9 already approved for some conditions and C5aR antagonists in development [N2-F2]. The JCI review similarly concludes that developing drugs aimed at diminishing local complement expression and activation could provide a novel approach to managing CKD [N3-F1]. These findings suggest that complement targeting may improve prognosis by reducing inflammation, oxidative stress, and fibrosis [N2-F2][N3-F1]. The evidence also indicates that complement activation is associated with AKI and its transition to CKD, implying that biomarkers of complement activation could help identify patients at higher risk of progression [N1-F3][N2-F2]. However, the evidence also notes that key mechanistic questions remain, particularly regarding complement’s interplay with other pathways such as the gut-kidney axis and metabolic comorbidities [N2-F2]. This suggests that while therapeutic targeting and biomarker use are promising, they should be interpreted with caution and integrated into broader clinical evaluation [N2-F2][N3-F1].

## 5) Complement regulation and disease heterogeneity across kidney conditions

Complement regulation differs in glomerular versus interstitial disease. In glomerular disease, the evidence highlights that uncontrolled complement activation can cause or contribute to glomerular injury in multiple kidney diseases, including C3 glomerulopathy and atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) [N1-F3]. It also notes that complement activation can occur independently of immune complex deposition, as in focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) and diabetic kidney disease (DKD) [N1-F3]. In interstitial disease, the evidence is more broadly framed around tubulointerstitial fibrosis and the AKI-to-CKD transition. The JCI review states that local complement activation is frequently observed in kidney disease, but its role in glomerular versus interstitial disease may differ [N3-F1]. In the experimental models, C3 deficiency reduced inflammation and fibrosis in multiple injury models, suggesting that complement regulation is a shared but potentially context-specific driver of both glomerular and interstitial injury [N3-F1]. The evidence also points to different complement pathways being activated in different diseases, such as lectin pathway activation in DKD and the broader classical/alternative pathways in AKI/CKD [N1-F3][N3-F1].

Complement inhibitors and regulators are important in shaping disease course. The evidence shows that inhibition of C5b-9 and C5aR can reduce inflammation and fibrosis in experimental models [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-F1]. The review also states that complement inhibition is a promising therapeutic strategy in renal diseases, with monoclonal antibodies targeting C5b-9 already approved for some conditions and C5aR antagonists in development [N2-F2]. Complement regulators such as factor H and complement factor I are also relevant because dysregulation of the complement system leads to renal disease through overproduction of anaphylatoxins or inappropriate formation of MAC [N6-R3]. The evidence further indicates that complement dysregulation can be associated with hemolytic uremic syndrome and more common glomerular diseases, underscoring the importance of complement regulation in disease progression [N6-R4]. In the AKI-to-CKD transition, dysregulated complement activation can persist even after the acute injury phase, contributing to sustained inflammation and fibrosis [N3-F1].

The evidence supports the idea that complement-related heterogeneity contributes to differences in AKI/CKD outcomes. First, the review emphasizes that the pathogenesis of AKI is highly complex, and complement involvement varies across AKI subtypes [N2-F2]. Second, the JCI review notes that the AKI-to-CKD transition remains poorly understood because of the complexity and heterogeneity of the kidney’s cellular composition [N3-F1]. Third, the evidence shows that failed-repair PTCs and reprogrammed C1Q+CD163+ macrophages are conserved features across mouse and human species and contribute to kidney injury [N3-F1]. These findings suggest that complement activation may not act in the same way across all AKI subtypes and CKD subtypes, leading to different patterns of injury, repair, and progression. The evidence also indicates that biomarkers such as C3 may be useful for identifying patients at risk of progression, but the exact role of complement in different subtypes is still being clarified [N1-F3][N2-F2][N3-F1].

## 6) Integrated conclusion

In summary, complement activation contributes to renal fibrosis and the progression from AKI to CKD through several linked mechanisms: inflammation, oxidative stress, myofibroblast activation, and persistent fibrotic remodeling. C3a, C5a, MAC, and complement receptors such as C3aR and C5aR1 are central to this process [N1-F3][N1-R4][N2-F2][N3-R2]. Experimental evidence strongly supports complement as a causal driver of renal fibrosis, with genetic complement deficiency and complement inhibition reducing inflammation and fibrosis in multiple models [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5][N3-F1]. The transition from AKI to CKD is shaped by persistent tissue injury, failed repair, and ongoing complement activation, with failed-repair PTCs and upregulated complement components such as C1q and C3 playing a major role [N3-F1]. Clinically, complement-driven CKD is relevant across glomerular and tubulointerstitial disease subtypes, and complement-derived biomarkers such as C3 are being explored for monitoring progression and prognosis [N1-F3][N2-F2][N5-R5]. Complement regulation differs by disease type, and complement inhibitors and regulators may modulate disease course, but dysregulation remains an important driver of renal injury [N2-F2][N6-R3]. Overall, complement activation is a key player in both the immediate injury response and the long-term progression to fibrosis and CKD, with strong translational support for targeting complement as a strategy to prevent or slow disease [N2-F2][N3-F1][N1-F3].
